summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but a visitor to Tacna faces a legal regime with no gender-identity-recognition law and no hate-crime statute. Anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label applied by investigators carries no separate legal consequence. Peru's Congress removed LGBT protections from the Penal Code's hate-crime provisions in 2017, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. Peru's compliance is contested. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights carried the case of Azul Rojas Marín to the Court, and in December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of the trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. Per BBC News Mundo it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Restrictions on trans people's use of public spaces are now legislated and are enforced beyond state facilities. In February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity and implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement reaches private life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected; its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected. The Public Prosecutor's Office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021, most victims gay men at 55.8% and trans women at 36.4%.

On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of the 'Los 5 Titos' hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She entered the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later carrying a white bag; the body was discovered by hostel staff when the rental time expired. Police were analysing surveillance footage inside and outside the hostel to trace the suspect's escape route and held camera footage and taxi-driver testimony, but per the audited reporting no suspect had been identified, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. Her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil on 23 May 2025 demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives.

Activists note a recently promulgated legislative proposal by congressman Alejandro Muñante restricting access to public bathrooms on grounds of sexual orientation, further tightening the space trans visitors and residents occupy in the region.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The legal architecture that reaches a trans visitor in Tacna is national rather than regional: the 2025 bathroom statute, the 2017 repeal of hate-crime coverage, the 2024 health-guidance revision and the July 2025 constitutional ruling all originate in Lima institutions and apply to Tacna on the same terms.

Regional comparison places Peru at the restrictive end of its neighbourhood. With Paraguay and Guyana it is one of three South American countries whose hate-crime law carries no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, while Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights obliges states in the region to guarantee trans people's full rights on the basis of personal autonomy.

Recorded indicators understate exposure. Gianna Camacho's co-authored 2024 reporting describes official hate-crime figures as a sub-registry, and the Public Prosecutor's Office count of 84 LGTB death complaints between January 2012 and May 2021 predates the 2024 finding that trans women are the group most affected by rising violence.

Enforcement of the bathroom regime has already been tested against private actors and against a sitting parliamentarian, which suggests that a trans visitor in Tacna may encounter the restriction in hostels, gyms, restaurants and transport rather than only in state buildings.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tacna face a documented enforcement gap in exactly the cases that reach them. No suspect had been identified in the killing of Marcia Paucara Cora as of the audited reporting, and the investigation was proceeding as a possible hate crime under a Penal Code that offers no separate hate-crime charge, meaning any eventual prosecution would proceed as ordinary homicide.

Local LGBT collectives have organised publicly around the killing, holding a vigil on 23 May 2025 and characterising the violence as structural rather than incidental, a framing that local residents can expect to recur in collective response to further cases.

For resident trans people the April 2025 statute, the pending Muñante proposal and the precedent set by the dismissed gym complaint combine to restrict facility access in both public and commercial premises, while the article 4 content ban and the obscenity sentencing increase constrain local media, advertising, artistic and educational work.

Healthcare access carries a documented improvement in terminology as of June 2024, though the practical availability of trans-competent care in Tacna itself is not established by the available sources.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory addresses trans-specific facility policy in Tacna's hostels, health services, police stations or places of detention, nor the treatment of trans detainees.

The reporting on the Azul Rojas Marín case, including the December 2025 sentencing and the characterisation of the case as the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination matter in the region, is attributed to BBC News Mundo and is not independently corroborated within this inventory.
